newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr relieved inflation is not dead.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr relieved inflation is not dead.

text.p: The Australian dollar recouped 1/4 cent of early losses at the midsession after inflation data were not so weak as to greatly raise the risk of a rate cut.

The headline consumer price index rose 0.2 percent in the March quarter taking annual growth to a four-year low of 1.3 percent from 1.5 percent in Q4, but this was a little above median forecasts of a 0.1 percent gain.

Furthermore the key underlying rate of inflation stayed at 2.1 percent for the year, whereas some had looked for a dip below the Reserve Bank's 2-3 percent target band, an event which would have certainly stoked speculation of an easing.
By 12.15 pm (0215 GMT) the dollar had scampered back up to US$0.7765/70 having slid to US$0.7745/50 just before the data hit dealing screens from an early US$0.7770/75.

The currency was also ahead of Tuesday's late US$0.7755/60 and comfortably above key support at US$0.7720. Resistance had proved tough at US$0.7795, however, with rumours of many offshore offers around there.

Traders said the bounce had been aided by sizeable demand out of Tokyo which reinforced talk Japanese funds were developing a taste for Australian government bonds. The dollar was up at 98.10/20 yen from 97.65/75 late here Tuesday.
It also remained firm on the mark, which had been undermined by a German economic institutes report predicting it would average 1.8000 per US$ in 1998, at 1.3319/28 from 1.3204/18.

The local unit had looked less secure against the U.S. dollar, however, as a steady decline in domestic yields eroded its traditional interest rate advantage. Indeed, recent weak employment data and Tuesday's benign result from the national minimum wage talks had some in the market betting the RBA may yet ease official rates for the fourth time this cycle.
The June 90-day bank bill future had risen as high as 94.17 this morning, for a 14 basis point gain in less than 24 hours.
They point to strengthening leading indicators in the economy which augur well for a pick up as the year progresses and feel a cut would be too pro-cyclical for the RBA's taste.

That view might change if the real side of the economy, and particularly employment, disappointed in the next month or so. The next monthly jobs report is due on May 8, which also happens to be the day RBA governor Ian Macfarlane gives his first testimony on the economy to a parliamentary committee.
To add extra spice the bank's policy board holds its monthly meeting on May 6, so that week is shaping up as a crucial one for interest rates. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
